No—**MiniMax M2.7 is text-only**, not natively multimodal. It accepts text (including code) and produces text; it does not directly take images, audio, or video as inputs.[1][2]

It is aimed at coding, long-context reasoning, tool use, and agentic workflows rather than vision or voice. For a multimodal MiniMax workflow, you would need to pair it with a separate image/video/audio model or convert those inputs to text first.[3][4]

Yes—**MiniMax M3 is natively multimodal**. It accepts **text, images, and video** as inputs and produces text output; MiniMax also says it can operate a desktop computer in agent workflows.[1][2]

## M3 at a glance

| Capability | MiniMax M3 |
|---|---|
| Input modalities | Text, image, video [2] |
| Output | Text [2] |
| Context window | Up to 1 million tokens [3] |
| Architecture | Mixture-of-Experts: about 428B total parameters, ~23B active [3] |
| Main focus | Coding agents, tool use, long-document/context work, visual and long-video understanding [2][1] |
| Video support | Long-form video understanding, reported up to 30 minutes in NVIDIA’s model reference [2] |

## Difference from M2.7

M2.7 is primarily a text/code reasoning model. M3 adds native visual understanding—trained jointly on text, image, and video from the beginning rather than attaching vision later—while also expanding the context capability to 1M tokens.[3][1]

A useful application: send it a screen recording plus a repository’s logs and ask it to identify a UI failure, trace the likely code path, and propose a patch.
